content: The transmission of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is zoonotic, with Leishmania infantum identified as the causative species. However, the data supporting this are derived from open-label, uncontrolled studies. Various treatment regimens have been employed, primarily involving pentavalent antimonials (20 mg/kg per day every 3–4 weeks), amphotericin B (either liposomal amphotericin B [L-AMB] or amphotericin B lipid complex) at 3–5 mg/kg per day for 3–4 weeks, or pentamidine (4 mg/kg per day [300 mg for an adult]) administered every 3–4 weeks. The effectiveness of secondary prophylaxis using amphotericin B lipid complex (3 mg/kg per day every 21 days) was evaluated in a single prospective randomized study, which compared it to no secondary prophylaxis. The drug was well-tolerated, and after 12 months of follow-up, 22% of patients receiving secondary prophylaxis experienced relapse, compared to 50% of those without prophylaxis. A meta-analysis of available studies demonstrated a clear benefit of secondary prophylaxis in reducing VL relapse rates. The average relapse rate was 67% in patients without secondary prophylaxis and 31% in those who received it. Most of the data originated from L. infantum-endemic areas where VL transmission is zoonotic. European studies suggest that a CD4 cell count greater than 100 cells/mm³ at the time of VL diagnosis reduces the likelihood of relapse. Consequently, for Spanish patients, a CD4 cell count threshold of 200–350 cells/mm³ was proposed as a safe criterion for discontinuing secondary prophylaxis. Similarly, in the Americas, liposomal amphotericin B is recommended for secondary prophylaxis in VL-HIV co-infected patients after the first VL episode, particularly in those with a CD4 T-cell count below 350/mm³. This recommendation is based on strong consensus but very low-certainty evidence. In endemic areas with anthroponotic transmission of Leishmania donovani, such as East Africa and Southeast Asia, the virulence of the parasite appears to be higher. For example, in a study conducted in Ethiopia, 11 out of 39 patients with relapse had a CD4 cell count above 200 cells/mm³ before relapse, whereas in Europe, relapse was uncommon in patients with a CD4 count above 100 cells/mm³. This suggests that L. donovani may exhibit greater virulence in anthroponotic transmission areas. Other contributing factors could include host immune responses, nutritional status, and the presence of co-infections or comorbidities. Despite greater clinical experience in managing HIV-VL co-infected patients in East Africa compared to Southeast Asia, evidence on secondary prophylaxis remains limited in both regions. More studies and clinical trials are urgently needed. Medical care for VL in HIV co-infected patients is severely restricted in these areas, with only a few tertiary referral centers managing such cases. Additionally, health systems, surveillance, and medical services for monitoring drug toxicity and patient follow-up are suboptimal. The risk of developing drug resistance must also be considered, as HIV co-infected patients may serve as reservoirs for drug-resistant L. donovani. To mitigate this risk, it is generally recommended to use a drug different from the one employed for treating the primary VL episode for secondary prophylaxis. Further research is necessary to establish criteria for initiating and discontinuing secondary prophylaxis and to identify the most effective single-dose drug for secondary prophylaxis in anthroponotic VL caused by L. donovani. Physicians should exercise caution when assessing patients with a history of multiple VL episodes prior to their HIV status being known. Factors such as migratory status, social and gender barriers, and health-seeking behavior should also be considered, as these may increase the risk of relapses going unnoticed and untreated. Delayed diagnosis and incomplete treatment, often due to non-compliance or cost-related issues, can also elevate the risk of relapse. In East Africa, data on secondary prophylaxis were derived from two open-label, non-comparative prospective cohort studies conducted in northwest Ethiopia. Pentamidine was provided as secondary prophylaxis to HIV-positive primary VL patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³ at the end of VL treatment and to relapsed VL patients regardless of their CD4 count. Pentamidine prophylaxis was initiated one month after completing VL treatment, provided no parasites were detected in tissue aspiration post-treatment. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis were part of routine care. In one study, 74 participants received monthly infusions of 4 mg/kg pentamidine isethionate diluted in normal saline for 12 months. After two years of follow-up, five out of 71 patients died, and the estimated probability of relapse-free survival was 79% at six months, 71% at one year, and 53% at 24–36 months. Serious adverse events were reported in 23% of patients, with two cases of renal failure potentially linked to pentamidine. In Southeast Asia, the only available data on secondary prophylaxis came from a retrospective cohort study in eastern India. Twenty-seven patients received amphotericin B (AMB) or liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) monthly, and their outcomes were compared to 24 patients who received no secondary prophylaxis. At one year of follow-up, none of the patients receiving secondary prophylaxis had relapsed, whereas 75% of the control group had. The authors concluded that monthly AMB might be effective in preventing relapse and mortality in VL-HIV patients, although the evidence was considered very uncertain. The World Health Organization (WHO) conditionally recommends secondary prophylaxis after the first episode of VL in HIV co-infected patients in East Africa. The choice of drugs is limited, with pentamidine being the primary option. Pentamidine has additional benefits, such as preventing Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, and is not currently used as a first-line drug for primary VL in areas with anthroponotic transmission. The use of a drug not routinely employed for primary VL treatment or relapses is theoretically advantageous in preventing drug resistance. However, the cost of pentamidine should be considered, as there is no donation program for VL. In the long term, its use may result in cost savings by preventing recurrent disease and associated morbidity and mortality. In terms of treatment outcomes, cure is defined as the absence of VL signs or symptoms after treatment, along with clinical improvement and a negative parasitological test of cure. For HIV co-infected patients, parasitological examination at the end of treatment is recommended, depending on feasibility. Repeated tests should only be performed in referral centers with surgical and blood transfusion services available. After treatment, VL cases are assessed twice to determine cure, treatment failure, relapse, death, or loss to follow-up.
